lines.trans: Chef, why did you get so drunk?
I am not drunk, but drank a little aperitif.
You can barely stand on your feet.
The face of the restaurant arrived, I am ready to welcome guests!
In this state you will not go out to the guests!
And you will never get married.
Stop grabbing me so roughly.

words.gram: future, 3rd person singular, perfective; хватит! = enough!

lines.trans: I must personally check our restaurant.
Do something with this drunken monster!
I had a very good idea.
What other idea can there be now?
Let us all together inspect the bar!

And you will never get married.
Stop grabbing me so roughly.

Do something with this drunken monster!

lines.trans: I must personally check our restaurant.
Do something with this drunken monster!
I had a very good idea.
What other idea can there be now?
Let us all together inspect the bar!
Let us all together inspect the bar!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'what for'.

examples.trans: What have you come for?
What's that for?
Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You're greedy!
Have you got any more?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strongly'.

examples.trans: I loved him so much!
The wind is blowing hard outside.

examples.text: Я так два года потеряла. Любила так сильно!
examples.trans: I lost two years like that. I loved him so much!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'питься'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'get drunk'.

examples.text: Шеф, зачем ты так сильно напился?
examples.trans: Chef, why did you get so drunk?

examples.text: Я не напился, а выпил немного аперитива.
examples.trans: I am not drunk, but drank a little aperitif.
Let me guess. You'll get drunk?

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

выпить.gloss: to drink, to have a drink

meanings.en: to drink up, to have a drink
meanings.note: often used without an object for drinking alcohol

examples.trans: Oh, I've had a bit to drink now.
Drink some water.
May I drink a tiny drop of beer?

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'много'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.
I'm a bit tired.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'apéritif' (from Late Latin 'aperitivus', 'opening' the appetite, from 'aperire', to open).

examples.text: Я не напился, а выпил немного аперитива.
examples.trans: I am not drunk, but drank a little aperitif.

examples.text: Официант предложил гостям лёгкий аперитив перед ужином.
examples.trans: The waiter offered the guests a light aperitif before dinner.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'barely'.

examples.trans: I can barely make ends meet.
I barely got up this morning.
Arkashka, you're barely washing!

meanings.note: the infinitive 'Стоять!' as a police order
the infinitive 'Стоять!' as a police order

examples.trans: I'm standing here.

examples.text: То есть просто стоять и смотреть?
examples.trans: So we just stand and watch?

examples.text: Стоять на месте, никто не выходит из кухни без разрешения!
examples.trans: Freeze right there, nobody leaves the kitchen without permission!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: refers back to the subject: 'он держит своё слово' = he keeps his word

examples.trans: He keeps his word.
They are building their houses.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'leg', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('foot') (Russian uses one word for both) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The right foot.
My leg hurts.

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'face', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('person, individual') (formal) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: It really suits you!
He has a very kind face.

examples.text: Карамельно-сливочный цвет. Очень тебе к лицу! Надень куртку.
examples.trans: A caramel-cream colour. It really suits you! Put the jacket on.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'быть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'arrive, increase'.

examples.text: Лицо ресторана прибыло, я готов встречать гостей!
examples.trans: The face of the restaurant arrived, I am ready to welcome guests!

examples.text: Главный гость уже прибыл, мы готовы подавать закуски!
examples.trans: The main guest has already arrived, we are ready to serve the appetizers!

examples.text: Поезд из Воронежа должен прибыть на вокзал ровно в девять утра.
examples.trans: The train from Voronezh is due to arrive at the station at nine in the morning sharp.

meanings.note: usually the short form: я готов (m), я готова (f)

examples.trans: I'm ready!
Lunch is ready.
Right, I'm ready!

meanings.en: to meet, to greet, to pick up
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'тречать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to meet, to welcome', paired with 'встретить'.

examples.text: Вас и не должны были встречать.
examples.trans: Nobody was supposed to meet you.

examples.text: Он всегда встречает гостей у двери.
examples.trans: He always greets guests at the door.

examples.text: Это не накладка. Вас и не должны были встречать.
examples.trans: That's not a mix-up. Nobody was supposed to meet you.

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.
You have visitors!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: 'что я за мэр такой' = what kind of mayor am I
Secondary conversational sense ('? = what's this?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: What is this?
He's so kind.
Pavel Yuryevich, what is this?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'остояние'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'condition, state' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Checking the condition of the wall.
In good condition.

examples.text: Эксперты уже начали проверку состояния старой стены.
examples.trans: Experts have already begun checking the condition of the old wall.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.
I'm going to Mum's.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

выйти.gloss: to go out, to get out

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go out, to get out', paired with 'выходить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to get out (be released)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks.
He left the house.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: used with verbs like выходить for marriage of a woman

examples.trans: She is marrying the neighbor.
He asked me to marry him and come to Moscow!

examples.text: Она вышла замуж в прошлом году.
examples.trans: She got married last year.

meanings.note: used with не before the verb, or alone

examples.text: Я никогда не был на море.
examples.trans: I've never been to the sea.
No! Never!

examples.text: Я никогда в жизни не пробовал такой вкусной утки!
examples.trans: I have never in my life tasted such delicious duck!

meanings.note: impersonal, + genitive: денег не хватило = there wasn't enough money
Secondary conversational sense ('that's enough!') (хватит!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: There wasn't enough money.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

examples.text: Хватит спорить из-за пустяков, давайте лучше спокойно работать!
examples.trans: Enough arguing over trifles, let us just work calmly instead!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Don't talk so rudely.
That's rude.

examples.text: А что вы так грубо разговариваете?
examples.trans: Why are you talking so rudely?

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'grab, clutch at'.

examples.text: Хватит за меня так грубо хвататься.
examples.trans: Stop grabbing me so roughly.

examples.text: Хватит в панике хвататься за все дела одновременно!
examples.trans: Stop frantically grabbing at every task at the same time!

examples.text: Макс готов хвататься за любую сложную работу на кухне.
examples.trans: Max is ready to jump at any difficult job in the kitchen.

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have to work.
Greed should be moderate.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Аникеев лично сюда приезжал, и что?
examples.trans: Anikeev came here in person, and what?
I know him personally.

examples.text: Пятнадцать лет мы просим новое здание! Аникеев лично сюда приезжал, и что?
examples.trans: For fifteen years we've been asking for a new building! Anikeev came here in person, and what?

meanings.en: to check, to test, to verify
meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'верить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to check, to test', paired with 'проверять'.

examples.trans: Check the soldering iron.
We'll check everything right now.

examples.text: Вот с таким настроением и иди к Аникееву. Паяльник проверь.
examples.trans: Go to Anikeev in just that mood. Check the soldering iron.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to do', forming an aspectual pair with 'делать'.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
I'll do it tomorrow.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: any thing at all, not a particular one

examples.trans: Say something.

examples.text: Правда, Нин, всё нормально. Скажи что-нибудь, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Honestly, Nina, everything's fine. Say something, please.
Are you doing anything about it?

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('drunk').

examples.trans: And we were drunk.
He came home drunk.

examples.text: Тогда была моя ошибка. И мы были пьяные.
examples.trans: Back then it was my mistake. And we were drunk.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'monster, beast' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Сделайте что-нибудь с этим пьяным чудовищем!
examples.trans: Do something with this drunken monster!

examples.text: Сделайте же наконец что-нибудь с этим шумным чудовищем!
examples.trans: Do something at last with this noisy monster!

examples.text: Когда шеф злится, он кажется стажёрам настоящим чудовищем.
examples.trans: When the chef gets angry, he seems like a real monster to the interns.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
He's at our place.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.en: to appear, to show up, to turn up
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'явиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to appear, to show up', paired with 'появляться'.

examples.text: Пусть только ещё раз здесь появится!
examples.trans: Let him just show up here one more time!
We came up with a good idea.

examples.text: Я тебе серьёзно говорю. Пусть только ещё раз здесь появится!
examples.trans: I'm telling you seriously. Let him just show up here one more time!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
It's very hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.trans: A good day.
What a lovely morning!

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'idea' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Good idea!

examples.text: Хорошая идея! Я сейчас же попробую.
examples.trans: Good idea! I will try right now.
I have an excellent idea!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('what') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
in exclamations: какой грязный! = how dirty!

examples.trans: What is your town like?
What a beautiful house!

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: in threats: ты ещё увидишь = you'll see
Secondary conversational sense ('still, yet') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('even (with comparatives)') (ещё больше = even more) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'can', forming an aspectual pair with 'смочь'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'идти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: May I go?
Let's go home.
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'together'.

examples.trans: We're together.
We live together.

examples.text: Мы с Пашей вместе уже месяц.
examples.trans: Pasha and I have been together for a month now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'инспектировать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'inspect'.

examples.text: А пойдёмте все вместе проинспектируем бар!
examples.trans: Let us all together inspect the bar!

examples.text: А пойдёмте сейчас все вместе проинспектируем наш бар!
examples.trans: Let us all go together right now and inspect our bar!

examples.text: Шеф решил лично проинспектировать чистоту каждого холодильника.
examples.trans: The chef decided to personally inspect the cleanliness of every refrigerator.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bar, pub' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Our bar is closing.

examples.text: Проверьте все бары и старых друзей.
examples.trans: Check all the bars and old friends.
It is already morning. Our bar is closing.
